title: The swimmer at the falls
hookLine: Confucius watches a man swim a torrent by going in with the whirl and out with the swirl (Zhuangzi 19)

cards: A rip current pulls a swimmer away from the beach, and the instinct is to fight it: swim straight back to shore, as hard as possible. Lifeguards warn that this is what wears swimmers out.

In the book of Zhuangzi, Confucius and his students are walking near a huge waterfall. The water pours down from an enormous height, and the rapids below foam for miles. No fish, no turtle could swim there.
And then Confucius sees a man in the water.

teach.b: Confucius is sure the man is in trouble, or trying to end his life. He sends his students running along the bank to pull him out.
But a few hundred paces downstream, the man climbs out by himself, shakes out his hair, and strolls along the bank, singing. Confucius hurries after him. I thought you were a ghost, he says.
Do you have a special way of treading water? No, the man says, I have no special way.

teach.h: DOWN WITH THE SWIRL, UP WITH THE EDDY.
teach.b: I go down with the swirl, and come up with the eddy. I follow the way of the water, and don't put anything of my own on it. That's how I stay afloat.
The Zhuangzi borrows Confucius as a character in several of its stories, and these are teaching tales, not records of the real Confucius. Today's word is the idea at the center: wu wei.
It's often translated doing nothing, but that's misleading. The swimmer isn't doing nothing. He's swimming a waterfall.
Wu wei is action without forcing: moving with the grain of things, the way Cook Ding's knife found the gaps. The Tao Te Ching loves water for this.
In James Legge's 1891 translation: "The highest excellence is like (that of) water."
Elsewhere the same book says nothing is softer than water, yet nothing does better against the hard and strong. And look back at this week. Wùhuà.
Cook Ding's knife. The useless tree. The joy of fish.
Drumming on the pot. The old man's horse. The swimmer.
Seven Taoist stories, and each one stops fighting the current.

how: Wu wei is a central idea in Taoism, found in the Tao Te Ching and the Zhuangzi; Taoist practitioners cultivate it through meditation, tai chi and qigong, and through a way of acting that follows the grain of things.

o: a Chinese way of swimming in rough water
acting without forcing, moving with how things go
doing nothing at all and letting life drift by

games.q: you're swimming below a huge waterfall, and the water is pulling you under. what do you do?
o: fight straight back to the bank.
go down with the swirl and come up with the eddy.
cling to a rock and wait.
games.why: the swimmer follows the water without imposing himself on it, climbs out downstream, and walks off singing.

practice: Notice where you're clenching right now, jaw, shoulders, hands, and let the breath go down with the swirl and come up with the eddy, all on its own; you don't have to breathe it.
Then think of one thing you've been forcing, a conversation, a plan, a person, and ask: where is the current actually going? What would it look like to swim with it?

wordCard.voice: Wu wei. Chinese for action without forcing: moving with the way things go, like the swimmer in the falls.

orig.note: Chinese, wú wéi: literally not doing, meaning action without forcing, a central word of Taoism.

carryVoice: Your line: go with the water. The swimmer let the falls carry him, and climbed out singing. That's the Taoist week.
